newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds firm on back of U.S. data/stronger punt.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds firm on back of U.S. data/stronger punt.

text.p: Irish bonds firmed in strong trade on Thursday, following European bond markets higher on the back of weaker-than-expected U.S. retail sales data, dealers said.
"Irish bonds have received an extra boost from a very strong Irish pound today," a dealer said. "We've seen curve-steepening and particularly good demand for the short end bonds."
By 1505 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was up 34.5 pence at 101.77 to yield 6.02 percent, while the eight percent bond due 2006 was up 45 pence at 109.10 to yield 6.63 percent.
Yields against German Bunds were broadly unchanged at 167 basis points over in the five-year bond, and 92 over in the 10-year.

Data released on Thursday showed U.S. retail sales dipped by 0.1 percent in May compared with expectations of a 0.4 percent rise, calming fears of inflationary pressure in the economy and allaying worries of an interest rate rise at the next FOMC meeting on July 2.
Bond and share markets pushed higher on the news, with U.S. bonds jumping almost a full point.
Meanwhile, the Irish pound gained more than a pfennig on the mark on a reversal of convergence play as doubts over EMU's start date gathered momentum, dealers said.
"This has really helped the short end, and tickled foreign interest," a dealer said.
Earlier this week a fresh bout of worries was triggered by a French call for more time to consider the EMU stability pact.
Since then, optimistic comments by European politicians about resolving difficulties at next week's EU summit in Amsterdam may have been shrugged off by some sectors of the market, a dealer said.
Irish CPI figures scheduled for release this morning have been delayed 24 hours for technical reasons, the Central Statistics Office said earlier.
The NTMA said on Thursday that it would auction on June 17 80 million Irish pounds of the 8.0 percent bond due 2006.
